items.title: Horn
items.description:
The 18th-century natural horn had no valves and produced notes from the natural harmonic series. Unlike the modern French horn, which has a fully chromatic range of about three and a half octaves, the 18th-century horn could produce only around sixteen natural notes. Its sound was also generally brighter and more open than that of the modern instrument.

The French horn formed part of the musical lives of Black people in eighteenth-century Britain. King, an enslaved man associated with William Franklin, was later taken in by a woman who arranged for him to receive tuition in both the French horn and violin. Ignatius Sancho (c. 1729–1780), one of the best-known Black residents of eighteenth-century London, later became a published composer, and some of his minuets included French horn parts. Although music could offer Black people a degree of independence and greater opportunities for cultural participation, they still lived within an unequal social structure.

items.title: Bartmann Bottle
items.description:
This Bartmann bottle was made in Frechen, Germany, around 1550–1700. Made from durable brown-glazed stoneware, it has a rounded body, narrow neck and sturdy handle for storing and carrying liquids. Its moulded flower medallion reflects the decorative style of Frechen stoneware, which was widely traded across Europe and commonly used in domestic and drinking settings.

The name Bartmann, meaning “bearded man” in German, refers to the distinctive bearded face moulded onto the neck of these vessels. In Britain, Bartmann vessels also became known as “Bellarmine” jugs, a name associated with the Catholic Cardinal Robert Bellarmine. Beyond their everyday use, some Bartmann bottles were later reused as “witch bottles”, filled with materials such as pins, nails or hair and concealed or buried as protective objects against witchcraft. Over time, this widely traded domestic object acquired additional religious, symbolic and ritual meanings within British social life.

items.title: Domino
items.description: This small ivory domino dates from the late 18th to early 19th century. Its value is marked by recessed circular pips on either side of the central dividing line. Dominoes were popular pieces for social tabletop games, and their hard ivory surfaces produced a distinctive click when placed or moved across a wooden table.

items.title: Punch Whistle
items.description:
This 19th-century whistle is made from white metal and shaped as Punch, the well-known comic character associated with British Punch and Judy performances. Although small and decorative, it was also designed to produce a clear, piercing whistle. Its combination of sound and playful figurative design reflects the popular entertainment culture of the period.

Punch developed from Pulcinella, a character from the Italian commedia dell’arte tradition, and became established in Britain from the seventeenth century. By the nineteenth century, Punch and Judy had become a familiar form of popular entertainment, with Punch’s humor often centered on disorder and exaggerated violence, including violence towards his wife Judy. Some nineteenth-century versions also included racial stereotypes, such as the character of Jim Crow, drawing on the blackface minstrel traditions of the period. Over time, the Punch has been increasingly criticized for their representations of domestic violence, racial stereotypes and violence in children’s entertainment.
